## Statement

Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. The benchmarking programs report this in graded form. What is cited downstream is a binary label, usually derived from interval overlap or direction agreement, and that label discards magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why two estimates differ: two studies estimating the same quantity imprecisely agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely disagree. No reported measure, graded or binary, separates estimand mismatch from random error, because doing so requires aligning the estimands first and then reporting a paired contrast with joint uncertainty, which no benchmarking report currently does as a matter of course.

## Why it is open

Separating estimand mismatch from random error requires a distributional claim about the trial's own error that trials do not publish, so the criterion that would do it cannot be computed from what is available. Aligning estimands before comparison is possible and expensive, and it reduces the number of comparable pairs, which is the resource benchmarking is short of. The binary label is also convenient for the audiences who cite benchmarking results, so the pressure to replace it runs the wrong way.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Wang SV, Schneeweiss S, RCT-DUPLICATE Initiative. Emulation of randomized clinical trials with nonrandomized database analyses: results of 32 clinical trials. JAMA 2023;329(16):1376-1385](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.4221) | Reports agreement across 32 prespecified emulations using several agreement metrics, which is the most careful existing treatment of the labeling question. |
| [Concordance between target trial emulation and randomised controlled trials: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 2025](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2025-086810) | Reports effect correlation and standardized-difference agreement across 107 pairs and relates concordance to specific design features rather than to a pass or fail label. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Align estimands before comparing, then report the paired contrast with joint uncertainty, heterogeneity and any prespecified tolerance that a categorical judgment would rest on, so a pass or fail is derived rather than assumed. Report ratio of effects, absolute effect difference, standardized agreement and prediction-interval coverage together, so estimand mismatch and random error remain separately visible. Prefer prospective forecasts of a trial's result to retrospective comparison, and replicate across databases as well as across questions, since a data source's calibration is what a decision maker needs.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.

**The source said.** "Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. Benchmarking nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label, usually derived from whether the confidence intervals overlap or whether the direction agrees. That label mixes estimand mismatch with random error: two studies estimating the same quantity with wide intervals will agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely will disagree. The reported statistic therefore does not measure what its users take it to measure."

**What was wrong with it.** The entry attributed the binary label to the benchmarking programs. They do not use one: RCT-DUPLICATE reports several agreement metrics and the 2026 concordance meta-analysis reports correlation and standardized agreement related to design features. The reduction to pass or fail happens downstream, in how those results are cited, which is a different and narrower claim.

**Dissent.** literature dissented (open): The entry criticizes binary replication labels. The concordance meta-analysis it draws on does not use one: it reports correlation and standardized-difference agreement and relates them to design features, which is the graded reporting the entry asks for. RCT-DUPLICATE similarly reports several agreement metrics. So the criticism lands on the citing practice rather than on the benchmarking literature, and the entry should say that. The part that survives is that a graded criterion still does not separate estimand mismatch from random error, since prediction-interval coverage requires a distributional claim about the trial's own error that trials do not publish. codex dissented (overstated): The criticism of confidence-interval overlap and sign agreement is technically sound, but the problem is framed too broadly. The agenda's own descriptions say that the cited benchmarks already report several graded metrics, including effect correlation and standardized differences, so benchmarking is not uniformly binary. Continuous effect differences, ratios, and standardized contrasts still cannot separate estimand mismatch from random error. That separation first requires commensurate estimands and then a joint sampling model incorporating uncertainty from both estimates, their covariance when applicable, and between-pair heterogeneity. Prediction-interval coverage does not require a trial to publish a full error distribution when an estimate and standard error or confidence interval are available, and coverage is itself calibrated across a suite rather than diagnosed from one pair. Ratios are additionally unstable when the reference effect is near zero. This is therefore partly an implementation and reporting problem with existing tools, not wholly an unresolved statistical-method problem; high severity is disproportionate unless the binary label is the sole basis for a decision. grok dissented (overstated): The claim that benchmarking “nonetheless reports success or failure as a binary label” is not faithful to the field’s primary programs or to the report’s own cited works. RCT-DUPLICATE and Franklin-line methods report regulatory/significance agreement, estimate agreement, and standardized-difference agreement together; the BMJ 2026 meta-analysis leads with Pearson correlation, ICC, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference agreement, and Bland–Altman, and only secondarily with binary metrics. Köppe, Micheloud, Erdmann, Heyard, and Held (2025) go further: they replace the two-trials (regulatory agreement) rule with the graded sceptical p-value, which uses both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision, and invert it to combined confidence intervals; they apply it to 29 RCT-DUPLICATE pairs. ISPOR Europe 2024 also floated enhanced multi-metric RCT–RWE agreement assessments for HTA. What remains open is universal adoption, explicit estimand alignment (how much estimand difference is tolerable), and routine prediction-interval coverage that treats trial sampling error as a distribution. Binary labels are still convenient for secondary citation and still appear beside continuous metrics, but they are not the sole or best existing practice. The report’s proposed direction (ratio of effects, absolute difference, standardized agreement, prediction-interval coverage, prospective forecasts) is largely what the better literature already does or is building.

Köppe, Micheloud, Erdmann, Heyard, and Held (2025) go further: they replace the two-trials (regulatory agreement) rule with the graded sceptical p-value, which uses both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision, and invert it to combined confidence intervals; they apply it to 29 RCT-DUPLICATE pairs. The report’s proposed direction (ratio of effects, absolute difference, standardized agreement, prediction-interval coverage, prospective forecasts) is largely what the better literature already does or is building.
    Cites 10.1001/jama.2023.4221: Already reports multiple agreement metrics (not a single pass/fail label) across 32 prespecified emulations; this is the report’s own cited “most careful existing treatment of the labeling question.”.
    Cites 10.1136/bmj-2025-086810: Primary reporting is continuous and multi-metric (correlation 0.59/0.83, ratio of ratios, standardized-difference rates, design-feature regressions), not a binary success label. Directly undercuts the claim that benchmarking only reports binary agreement..
    Cites arxiv:2412.09334: Supplies a graded, calibrated alternative to binary two-trials/regulatory agreement (the sceptical p-value), depending on both p-values, effect sizes, and relative precision; extends to non-inferiority and inverted CIs; applied to RCT-DUPLICATE. Partially delivers the report’s call for calibrated comparison rather than a binary label..
    Cites 10.1186/s12874-025-02589-z: Peer-reviewed publication of the sceptical p-value application to RWE emulations (same work as arXiv 2412.09334), confirming the graded metric is in the methods literature, not only a preprint..

glm
:   **open / supported.** The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It accurately characterizes a limitation in current practice: benchmarking often relies on binary labels (e.g., CI overlap) that conflate estimand mismatch with random error. The stated reasons for it being open (the difficulty of defining tolerable estimand differences and the convenience of binary labels) logically support the persistence of this practice. The claim is appropriately scoped as a critique of current reporting standards rather than an impossibility claim.

:   `R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R7:counter-and-support-both-present`
